summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of Kosovo, adopted on 9 April 2008 and in force from 15 June 2008, guarantees equality before the law, protects human dignity as inviolable, and under Article 24 prohibits discrimination on grounds that include gender and sexual orientation.

The Law on Protection from Discrimination has covered sexual orientation since 2004 and was amended on 26 May 2015, taking effect in July 2015, to add gender identity as a protected ground. Its coverage extends to employment, membership of organisations, education, provision of goods and services, social security and access to housing, and it defines discrimination to include direct and indirect discrimination, harassment, victimisation and segregation. An international rights organisation's overview updated in March 2026 reports that implementation of this framework remains inconsistent.

The Criminal Code in force from April 2019 provides additional penalties for hate crimes motivated by the victim's gender identity, and the same code provides additional penalties where the motive is the victim's sexual orientation.

Same-sex sexual intercourse has been legal in independent Kosovo since 2008; the 2004 international administration of the territory set the age of consent at 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation and made sexual offences gender-neutral.

There is no administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. A citizen who was refused a name and gender-marker change by the Civil Registration Agency filed suit in 2017 and requested constitutional review in July 2018, and in December 2019 the Basic Court of Pristina ruled in his favour, affirming the right to change both name and sex marker on identity documents without evidence of surgical intervention or any other medical change. The Ministry of Justice and the Civil Registration Agency stated that the judgment would not be treated as precedent and that other transgender people would have to pursue a similar court procedure. Reporting from January 2019 had already documented that gender recognition in Kosovo ran through the courts case by case.

Marriage under Article 14 of the Law on Family is defined as a legally registered community of two persons of different sexes. A Civil Code proposal providing for same-sex civil partnerships, tabled on 7 July 2020, was rejected by the Assembly on 16 March 2022 with 28 of 120 deputies voting in favour. The Prime Minister announced on 25 April 2024 an intention to legalise same-sex unions, but as of February 2026 Parliament had still not adopted the new Civil Code, amid fierce opposition that included members of the ruling party. A published analysis of the draft Civil Code's gender-neutral marriage language sets out what the text would permit if adopted.

Reporting to the authorities is limited: 10 bias-motivated crimes against LGBTQ people were reported to the authorities in 2019, with a further 13 reported only to LGBTQ organisations, and LGBTQ people tend not to report discrimination or abuse to the police. In February 2019 the authorities opened a case against a Ministry of Justice official who had called for LGBTQ people to be beheaded, and police took him into custody.

An LGBTQI+ organisation in Pristina provides free confidential legal aid and psychological support in person and through a dedicated app, offers reproductive and sexual health services including support for transgender people navigating hormonal procedures in cooperation with the Ministry, and runs free HIV testing. Free PrEP HIV-prevention treatment has been available at the QKUK Infectious Disease Clinic since 12 June 2024 following advocacy by that organisation.
tangentialFactors:
Regional comparison: the European Court of Human Rights ruled in X v FYROM, reported in January 2019, that Macedonia's requirement of surgery for a gender-marker change violates private-life rights. Kosovo's own applicant in the name-and-gender-change case followed that ruling closely while his case was pending.

Public organising is visible and documented. The first Pride parade in Pristina was held in May 2016, with an annual Pride Week since 2017; a local outlet reported a third annual Pride Parade with week-long exhibitions, conferences and discussions organised by the Center for Equality and Liberty. The October 2019 march through the capital, under the slogan 'Whoever your heart beats for', was held without incident but under multiple threats, with anonymous warnings in 2017 telling people not to attend. The 2024 Pride Week ran under the motto 'I love you as you are!'

Hostile speech is documented in the political sphere. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 records that CSGD's 2022 annual report found intolerance and hatred, with politicians' hate speech common during Civil Code debates, and that an artist received death threats over a painting. Reuters reported in May 2024 that the country was considering same-sex unions amid fierce opposition.

Prevalence figures in the inventory are dated and measured across LGBTQ people rather than transgender people specifically: a 2015 National Democratic Institute survey found 81% of LGBTQ+ Kosovars reported psychological abuse and 29% reported physical violence, and a separate NDI study found over 97% of respondents unwilling to accept a child who came out as lesbian or gay. These figures describe 2015 and the LGBTQ population as a whole.

A 2018 Blood Donation Week guideline bars from donation anyone who has 'intimate relationships with the same sex'. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people are permitted to serve openly in the military, though they may face discrimination from peers.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition for residents requires an individual court action. The December 2019 Basic Court of Pristina judgment established that gender identity can be recognised without proof of surgery or other medical change, but the Ministry of Justice and the Civil Registration Agency stated it would not be treated as precedent, so each subsequent applicant must litigate separately.

Residents who experience discrimination have statutory coverage across employment, membership of organisations, education, goods and services, social security and housing under the Law on Protection from Discrimination, with gender identity protected since July 2015, and additional penalties available under the April 2019 Criminal Code for hate crimes motivated by gender identity or sexual orientation.

Reporting practice among residents is split: of bias-motivated crimes against LGBTQ people in 2019, 10 were reported to the authorities and 13 only to LGBTQ organisations, reflecting a tendency not to approach the police.

CSGD operates free confidential legal aid and psychological support in person and via app.csgd-ks.org, provides reproductive and sexual health services including support for transgender people navigating hormonal procedures in cooperation with the Ministry, and offers free HIV testing. Free PrEP has been available at the QKUK Infectious Disease Clinic since 12 June 2024.

Marriage for residents remains restricted to couples of different sexes under Article 14 of the Law on Family, and the Civil Code that would change this had not been adopted as of February 2026.

The 2018 blood donation guideline excluding people with 'intimate relationships with the same sex' applies to residents donating blood, and open military service by lesbian, gay and bisexual personnel may be accompanied by peer discrimination.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the inventory contains both a flat statement that transgender people are not allowed to legally change their gender in Kosovo even after sex reassignment surgery, and a December 2019 Basic Court of Pristina judgment permitting a name and sex-marker change without medical evidence. The sources do not establish whether an administrative route exists at present, or whether that judgment has been applied to any later applicant.

Unresolved: whether the new Civil Code will be adopted is open. The inventory records a rejection in March 2022, an April 2024 government pledge, and non-adoption as of February 2026, with no later legislative outcome sourced.

Unresolved: no source in the inventory provides a trans-specific violence or killing figure with a population denominator, and no source separates transgender people's experiences from the LGBTQ-wide survey results of 2015. Trans-specific prevalence in Kosovo is therefore not sourced.

Not sourced: the inventory contains no material on border or airport screening treatment specific to transgender or gender-nonconforming travellers, on document-marker flagging at entry, or on how foreign identity documents bearing a changed gender marker are read by Kosovar authorities.

Not sourced: no source addresses transgender people's placement or treatment in police custody or detention, and none documents access to gender-affirming care for short-term visitors.
